hops.title: Say it: how a tree drinks
hops.text: Save this for the debrief, once the blue has climbed: "A tree drinks through its roots, and its leaves let the water go into the air, where we can't see it." Then look outside together. A tree can take up 10 to 150 gallons in a day, and about 95 percent of it goes back into the air.

sources.citation: Purdue University Forestry and Natural Resources Extension, "Purdue Landscape Report: How do trees use water?"
Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e (OpenStax), 30.5 Transport of Water and Solutes in Plants

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind looking up at the sunlit green leaves of a tall oak tree.
image.caption: A tree can take up gallons of water in a day, and most of it goes back into the air.

hops.title: Ask it: how does water reach the top of a redwood?
hops.text: Once the celery has turned blue, ask, "The tallest coast redwoods grow over 350 feet high, and trees have no heart to pump water. How does water get to the top?" Expect rain, giant straws, even squirrels with buckets. Enjoy every guess, then point at your leafy stalk and wonder aloud what its leaves were doing.

sources.citation: UF/IFAS Extension Pasco County, "Do Plants have a Vascular System?"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind standing at the base of towering reddish-brown coast redwood trees, looking up toward the high green branches.
image.caption: The tallest coast redwoods rise over 350 feet, and they lift water to the top without a pump.

hops.title: Compare it: a pop-up tissue box
hops.text: After you compare the leafy and leafless stalks, hand your child a pop-up tissue box. Pull one tissue out and the next one rises right behind it. Water in a plant's tiny tubes works much the same way: the water clings to itself, so when some dries off a leaf, it tugs the next bit up.

sources.citation: Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e (OpenStax), 30.5 Transport of Water and Solutes in Plants

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A child's hand pulling a white tissue from a pop-up box on a kitchen table, the next tissue rising behind it, beside a glass of blue water holding a celery stalk.
image.caption: Like pop-up tissues, water in a stem clings together, so water leaving the leaves tugs more up.
